This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines--> ==Overview== {{Infobox Shinto shrine | name = Tsugizakura Ōji | image = [[File:Tsugizakura-oji and Ippo Sugi.JPG|250px]] | caption = Torii gate of Tsugizakura Ōji and the "Ippo Sugi" cedar | location = 591 Nonaka, Nakahechi-chō, Tanabe City, Wakayama Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{coord|33|49|42.7|N|135|38|03.0|E|region:JP}} | deity = Unknown | established = Unknown | other_names = Next Sakura Ōji, Continued Sakura Ōji | festivals = }}
'''Tsugizakura Ōji''' (継桜王子), also known as '''Next Sakura Ōji''' (次桜王子) or '''Continued Sakura Ōji''' (続桜王子), is a Shinto shrine located in {{ill|Nakahechi, Tanabe|ja|田辺市中辺路町}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|ja|和歌山県}}, Japan. It is one of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}} shrines along the {{ill|Kumano Kodo|ja|熊野古道}} pilgrimage route. The site is part of the UNESCO World Heritage-listed "Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range" and is designated as a National Historic Site of Japan (2000) and part of the Scenic Beauty Site "Southern Mandala Landscape" (2015)<ref name="Tanabe">{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html|title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments|publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education|accessdate=2016-05-21}}</ref>.
== History == [[File:Monument TSUGIZAKURA-oji remains.JPG|thumb|right|150px|Tsugizakura Ōji monument]] Tsugizakura Ōji is mentioned as early as 1109 in the ''{{ill|Chūyūki|ja|中右記}}'' and later in Fujiwara no Teika's ''Kumano Dō no Maguki'' (part of the ''Meigetsuki'') in 1201. The shrine is thought to have originally been located east of its current site and was relocated during the early modern period. During the Edo period, it was known as ''Wakaichi Ōji Gongen'' and served as the local guardian shrine. In 1909, it was merged with Chikano Shrine but later restored to its original status after World War II<ref name="Nishi">Nishi [1987: 156]</ref>.
== Legends and Natural Features == The shrine is famous for the ''Tsugizakura'' (Grafted Sakura), believed to have grown from the graft of a cypress and a cherry tree. A legend connects the tree to {{ill|Fujiwara no Hidehira|ja|藤原秀衡}}, a lord of the Northern Fujiwara clan, who is said to have left his newborn son near the shrine during his pilgrimage to Kumano, praying that if the child survived, the tree would flourish.
Another notable feature is the ''Nonaka Ippo Sugi'' (One-Sided Cedar of Nonaka), a grove of ancient cedar trees that grow with their branches leaning in the same direction. These trees, some over 800 years old, were preserved through the efforts of the naturalist {{ill|Minakata Kumagusu|ja|南方熊楠}}, who opposed the government’s shrine consolidation policies during the Meiji period.
== Nonaka Spring (Selected 100 Exquisite Waters of Japan) == Beneath the shrine lies the ''Nonaka Spring'', known for its clear waters that have never dried up. It served as a rest stop for pilgrims and remains a local water source. The spring is designated as a natural monument of Tanabe City.
== Cultural Properties == * **National Designations:** * Part of the "Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range" (Historic Site, 2000) * Part of the "Southern Mandala Landscape" (Place of Scenic Beauty, 2015)
* **Wakayama Prefecture Designations:** * Nonaka Ippo Sugi - Prefectural Natural Monument (1958) * Nonaka Lion Dance - Prefectural Folk Cultural Property (1971)
== Access == * **Address:** 591 Nonaka, Nakahechi-chō, Tanabe City, Wakayama Prefecture, Japan * **Transport:** From {{ill|Kii-Tanabe Station|ja|紀伊田辺駅}}, take a bus to the "Nonaka Ippo Sugi" stop, then walk about 10 minutes.

'''{{PAGENAME}}''' is one of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|fr|Kujūkuōji|ja|九十九王子|lt=99 ōji Shrines}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. <!--PAGENAME magic word should be substituted in the future when this is moved to its final pagename. This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines--> ==Overview== {{Infobox Shinto shrine | name = Tsugizakura Ōji | image = [[File:Tsugizakura-oji and Ippo Sugi.JPG|250px]] | caption = Torii gate of Tsugizakura Ōji and the "Ippo Sugi" cedar | location = 591 Nonaka, Nakahechi-chō, Tanabe City, Wakayama Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{coord|33|49|42.7|N|135|38|03.0|E|region:JP}} | deity = Unknown | established = Unknown | other_names = Next Sakura Ōji, Continued Sakura Ōji | festivals = }}
'''Tsugizakura Ōji''' (継桜王子), also known as '''Next Sakura Ōji''' (次桜王子) or '''Continued Sakura Ōji''' (続桜王子), is a Shinto shrine located in {{ill|Nakahechi, Tanabe|ja|田辺市中辺路町}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|ja|和歌山県}}, Japan. It is one of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}} shrines along the {{ill|Kumano Kodo|ja|熊野古道}} pilgrimage route. The site is part of the UNESCO World Heritage-listed "Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range" and is designated as a National Historic Site of Japan (2000) and part of the Scenic Beauty Site "Southern Mandala Landscape" (2015)<ref name="Tanabe">{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html|title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments|publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education|accessdate=2016-05-21}}</ref>.
== History == [[File:Monument TSUGIZAKURA-oji remains.JPG|thumb|right|150px|Tsugizakura Ōji monument]] Tsugizakura Ōji is mentioned as early as 1109 in the ''{{ill|Chūyūki|ja|中右記}}'' and later in Fujiwara no Teika's ''Kumano Dō no Maguki'' (part of the ''Meigetsuki'') in 1201. The shrine is thought to have originally been located east of its current site and was relocated during the early modern period. During the Edo period, it was known as ''Wakaichi Ōji Gongen'' and served as the local guardian shrine. In 1909, it was merged with Chikano Shrine but later restored to its original status after World War II<ref name="Nishi">Nishi [1987: 156]</ref>.
== Legends and Natural Features == The shrine is famous for the ''Tsugizakura'' (Grafted Sakura), believed to have grown from the graft of a cypress and a cherry tree. A legend connects the tree to {{ill|Fujiwara no Hidehira|ja|藤原秀衡}}, a lord of the Northern Fujiwara clan, who is said to have left his newborn son near the shrine during his pilgrimage to Kumano, praying that if the child survived, the tree would flourish.
Another notable feature is the ''Nonaka Ippo Sugi'' (One-Sided Cedar of Nonaka), a grove of ancient cedar trees that grow with their branches leaning in the same direction. These trees, some over 800 years old, were preserved through the efforts of the naturalist {{ill|Minakata Kumagusu|ja|南方熊楠}}, who opposed the government’s shrine consolidation policies during the Meiji period.
== Nonaka Spring (Selected 100 Exquisite Waters of Japan) == Beneath the shrine lies the ''Nonaka Spring'', known for its clear waters that have never dried up. It served as a rest stop for pilgrims and remains a local water source. The spring is designated as a natural monument of Tanabe City.
== Cultural Properties == * **National Designations:** * Part of the "Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range" (Historic Site, 2000) * Part of the "Southern Mandala Landscape" (Place of Scenic Beauty, 2015)
* **Wakayama Prefecture Designations:** * Nonaka Ippo Sugi - Prefectural Natural Monument (1958) * Nonaka Lion Dance - Prefectural Folk Cultural Property (1971)
== Access == * **Address:** 591 Nonaka, Nakahechi-chō, Tanabe City, Wakayama Prefecture, Japan * **Transport:** From {{ill|Kii-Tanabe Station|ja|紀伊田辺駅}}, take a bus to the "Nonaka Ippo Sugi" stop, then walk about 10 minutes.

revision.text:
'''{{PAGENAME}}''' is one of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|fr|Kujūkuōji|ja|九十九王子|lt=99 ōji Shrines}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. <!--PAGENAME magic word should be substituted in the future when this is moved to its final pagename. This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines--> ==Overview== {{Infobox Shinto shrine | name = Tsugizakura Ōji | image = [[File:Tsugizakura-oji and Ippo Sugi.JPG|250px]] | caption = Torii gate of Tsugizakura Ōji and the "Ippo Sugi" cedar | location = 591 Nonaka, Nakahechi-chō, Tanabe City, Wakayama Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{coord|33|49|42.7|N|135|38|03.0|E|region:JP}} | deity = Unknown | established = Unknown | other_names = Next Sakura Ōji, Continued Sakura Ōji | festivals = }}
'''Tsugizakura Ōji''' (継桜王子), also known as '''Next Sakura Ōji''' (次桜王子) or '''Continued Sakura Ōji''' (続桜王子), is a Shinto shrine located in {{ill|Nakahechi, Tanabe|ja|田辺市中辺路町}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|ja|和歌山県}}, Japan. It is one of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}} shrines along the {{ill|Kumano Kodo|ja|熊野古道}} pilgrimage route. The site is part of the UNESCO World Heritage-listed "Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range" and is designated as a National Historic Site of Japan (2000) and part of the Scenic Beauty Site "Southern Mandala Landscape" (2015)<ref name="Tanabe">{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html|title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments|publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education|accessdate=2016-05-21}}</ref>.
== History == [[File:Monument TSUGIZAKURA-oji remains.JPG|thumb|right|150px|Tsugizakura Ōji monument]] Tsugizakura Ōji is mentioned as early as 1109 in the ''{{ill|Chūyūki|ja|中右記}}'' and later in Fujiwara no Teika's ''Kumano Dō no Maguki'' (part of the ''Meigetsuki'') in 1201. The shrine is thought to have originally been located east of its current site and was relocated during the early modern period. During the Edo period, it was known as ''Wakaichi Ōji Gongen'' and served as the local guardian shrine. In 1909, it was merged with Chikano Shrine but later restored to its original status after World War II<ref name="Nishi">Nishi [1987: 156]</ref>.
== Legends and Natural Features == The shrine is famous for the ''Tsugizakura'' (Grafted Sakura), believed to have grown from the graft of a cypress and a cherry tree. A legend connects the tree to {{ill|Fujiwara no Hidehira|ja|藤原秀衡}}, a lord of the Northern Fujiwara clan, who is said to have left his newborn son near the shrine during his pilgrimage to Kumano, praying that if the child survived, the tree would flourish.
Another notable feature is the ''Nonaka Ippo Sugi'' (One-Sided Cedar of Nonaka), a grove of ancient cedar trees that grow with their branches leaning in the same direction. These trees, some over 800 years old, were preserved through the efforts of the naturalist {{ill|Minakata Kumagusu|ja|南方熊楠}}, who opposed the government’s shrine consolidation policies during the Meiji period.
== Nonaka Spring (Selected 100 Exquisite Waters of Japan) == Beneath the shrine lies the ''Nonaka Spring'', known for its clear waters that have never dried up. It served as a rest stop for pilgrims and remains a local water source. The spring is designated as a natural monument of Tanabe City.
== Cultural Properties == * **National Designations:** * Part of the "Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range" (Historic Site, 2000) * Part of the "Southern Mandala Landscape" (Place of Scenic Beauty, 2015)
* **Wakayama Prefecture Designations:** * Nonaka Ippo Sugi - Prefectural Natural Monument (1958) * Nonaka Lion Dance - Prefectural Folk Cultural Property (1971)
== Access == * **Address:** 591 Nonaka, Nakahechi-chō, Tanabe City, Wakayama Prefecture, Japan * **Transport:** From {{ill|Kii-Tanabe Station|ja|紀伊田辺駅}}, take a bus to the "Nonaka Ippo Sugi" stop, then walk about 10 minutes.
== References == * {{Cite book|ja|author=Ue Toshikatsu|year=2004|title=World Heritage Kumano Kodo|publisher=Shinjuku Shobō|isbn=4880083216}} * {{Cite book|ja|editor=Kadokawa Japanese Place Name Dictionary Editorial Committee|year=1985|title=Wakayama Prefecture|publisher=Kadokawa Shoten|isbn=404001300X}} * {{Cite book|ja|author=Kumanonji Editorial Committee|year=1973|title=Ancient Roads and Ōji Shrines - Kumano Nakahechi|publisher=Kumano Nakahechi Publishing Association}}
== External Links == * [http://www.nakahechi.jp/saijiki.html Nakahechi Seasonal Events] - Official site of the Nakahechi Tourism Association * [http://www.pref.wakayama.lg.jp/prefg/000200/photomuseum/087.html Tsugizakura Ōji] - Wakayama Prefecture Photo Museum

'''{{PAGENAME}}''' is one of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|fr|Kujūkuōji|ja|九十九王子|lt=99 ōji Shrines}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. <!--PAGENAME magic word should be substituted in the future when this is moved to its final pagename. This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines--> ==Overview== {{Infobox Shinto shrine | name = Tsugizakura Ōji | image = [[File:Tsugizakura-oji and Ippo Sugi.JPG|250px]] | caption = Torii gate of Tsugizakura Ōji and the "Ippo Sugi" cedar | location = 591 Nonaka, Nakahechi-chō, Tanabe City, Wakayama Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{coord|33|49|42.7|N|135|38|03.0|E|region:JP}} | deity = Unknown | established = Unknown | other_names = Next Sakura Ōji, Continued Sakura Ōji | festivals = }}
'''Tsugizakura Ōji''' (継桜王子), also known as '''Next Sakura Ōji''' (次桜王子) or '''Continued Sakura Ōji''' (続桜王子), is a Shinto shrine located in {{ill|Nakahechi, Tanabe|ja|田辺市中辺路町}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|ja|和歌山県}}, Japan. It is one of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}} shrines along the {{ill|Kumano Kodo|ja|熊野古道}} pilgrimage route. The site is part of the UNESCO World Heritage-listed "Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range" and is designated as a National Historic Site of Japan (2000) and part of the Scenic Beauty Site "Southern Mandala Landscape" (2015)<ref name="Tanabe">{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html|title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments|publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education|accessdate=2016-05-21}}</ref>.
== History == [[File:Monument TSUGIZAKURA-oji remains.JPG|thumb|right|150px|Tsugizakura Ōji monument]] Tsugizakura Ōji is mentioned as early as 1109 in the ''{{ill|Chūyūki|ja|中右記}}'' and later in Fujiwara no Teika's ''Kumano Dō no Maguki'' (part of the ''Meigetsuki'') in 1201. The shrine is thought to have originally been located east of its current site and was relocated during the early modern period. During the Edo period, it was known as ''Wakaichi Ōji Gongen'' and served as the local guardian shrine. In 1909, it was merged with Chikano Shrine but later restored to its original status after World War II<ref name="Nishi">Nishi [1987: 156]</ref>.
== Legends and Natural Features == The shrine is famous for the ''Tsugizakura'' (Grafted Sakura), believed to have grown from the graft of a cypress and a cherry tree. A legend connects the tree to {{ill|Fujiwara no Hidehira|ja|藤原秀衡}}, a lord of the Northern Fujiwara clan, who is said to have left his newborn son near the shrine during his pilgrimage to Kumano, praying that if the child survived, the tree would flourish.
Another notable feature is the ''Nonaka Ippo Sugi'' (One-Sided Cedar of Nonaka), a grove of ancient cedar trees that grow with their branches leaning in the same direction. These trees, some over 800 years old, were preserved through the efforts of the naturalist {{ill|Minakata Kumagusu|ja|南方熊楠}}, who opposed the government’s shrine consolidation policies during the Meiji period.
== Nonaka Spring (Selected 100 Exquisite Waters of Japan) == Beneath the shrine lies the ''Nonaka Spring'', known for its clear waters that have never dried up. It served as a rest stop for pilgrims and remains a local water source. The spring is designated as a natural monument of Tanabe City.
== Cultural Properties == * **National Designations:** * Part of the "Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range" (Historic Site, 2000) * Part of the "Southern Mandala Landscape" (Place of Scenic Beauty, 2015)
* **Wakayama Prefecture Designations:** * Nonaka Ippo Sugi - Prefectural Natural Monument (1958) * Nonaka Lion Dance - Prefectural Folk Cultural Property (1971)
== Access == * **Address:** 591 Nonaka, Nakahechi-chō, Tanabe City, Wakayama Prefecture, Japan * **Transport:** From {{ill|Kii-Tanabe Station|ja|紀伊田辺駅}}, take a bus to the "Nonaka Ippo Sugi" stop, then walk about 10 minutes.

This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines--> ==Overview== {{Infobox Shinto shrine | name = Tsugizakura Ōji | image = [[File:Tsugizakura-oji and Ippo Sugi.JPG|250px]] | caption = Torii gate of Tsugizakura Ōji and the "Ippo Sugi" cedar | location = 591 Nonaka, Nakahechi-chō, Tanabe City, Wakayama Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{coord|33|49|42.7|N|135|38|03.0|E|region:JP}} | deity = Unknown | established = Unknown | other_names = Next Sakura Ōji, Continued Sakura Ōji | festivals = }}
'''Tsugizakura Ōji''' (継桜王子), also known as '''Next Sakura Ōji''' (次桜王子) or '''Continued Sakura Ōji''' (続桜王子), is a Shinto shrine located in {{ill|Nakahechi, Tanabe|ja|田辺市中辺路町}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|ja|和歌山県}}, Japan. It is one of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}} shrines along the {{ill|Kumano Kodo|ja|熊野古道}} pilgrimage route. The site is part of the UNESCO World Heritage-listed "Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range" and is designated as a National Historic Site of Japan (2000) and part of the Scenic Beauty Site "Southern Mandala Landscape" (2015)<ref name="Tanabe">{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html|title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments|publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education|accessdate=2016-05-21}}</ref>.
== History == [[File:Monument TSUGIZAKURA-oji remains.JPG|thumb|right|150px|Tsugizakura Ōji monument]] Tsugizakura Ōji is mentioned as early as 1109 in the ''{{ill|Chūyūki|ja|中右記}}'' and later in Fujiwara no Teika's ''Kumano Dō no Maguki'' (part of the ''Meigetsuki'') in 1201. The shrine is thought to have originally been located east of its current site and was relocated during the early modern period. During the Edo period, it was known as ''Wakaichi Ōji Gongen'' and served as the local guardian shrine. In 1909, it was merged with Chikano Shrine but later restored to its original status after World War II<ref name="Nishi">Nishi [1987: 156]</ref>.
== Legends and Natural Features == The shrine is famous for the ''Tsugizakura'' (Grafted Sakura), believed to have grown from the graft of a cypress and a cherry tree. A legend connects the tree to {{ill|Fujiwara no Hidehira|ja|藤原秀衡}}, a lord of the Northern Fujiwara clan, who is said to have left his newborn son near the shrine during his pilgrimage to Kumano, praying that if the child survived, the tree would flourish.
Another notable feature is the ''Nonaka Ippo Sugi'' (One-Sided Cedar of Nonaka), a grove of ancient cedar trees that grow with their branches leaning in the same direction. These trees, some over 800 years old, were preserved through the efforts of the naturalist {{ill|Minakata Kumagusu|ja|南方熊楠}}, who opposed the government’s shrine consolidation policies during the Meiji period.
== Nonaka Spring (Selected 100 Exquisite Waters of Japan) == Beneath the shrine lies the ''Nonaka Spring'', known for its clear waters that have never dried up. It served as a rest stop for pilgrims and remains a local water source. The spring is designated as a natural monument of Tanabe City.
== Cultural Properties == * **National Designations:** * Part of the "Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range" (Historic Site, 2000) * Part of the "Southern Mandala Landscape" (Place of Scenic Beauty, 2015)
* **Wakayama Prefecture Designations:** * Nonaka Ippo Sugi - Prefectural Natural Monument (1958) * Nonaka Lion Dance - Prefectural Folk Cultural Property (1971)
== Access == * **Address:** 591 Nonaka, Nakahechi-chō, Tanabe City, Wakayama Prefecture, Japan * **Transport:** From {{ill|Kii-Tanabe Station|ja|紀伊田辺駅}}, take a bus to the "Nonaka Ippo Sugi" stop, then walk about 10 minutes.

== History == [[File:Monument TSUGIZAKURA-oji remains.JPG|thumb|right|150px|Tsugizakura Ōji monument]] Tsugizakura Ōji is mentioned as early as 1109 in the ''{{ill|Chūyūki|ja|中右記}}'' and later in Fujiwara no Teika's ''Kumano Dō no Maguki'' (part of the ''Meigetsuki'') in 1201. The shrine is thought to have originally been located east of its current site and was relocated during the early modern period. During the Edo period, it was known as ''Wakaichi Ōji Gongen'' and served as the local guardian shrine. In 1909, it was merged with Chikano Shrine but later restored to its original status after World War II<ref name="Nishi">Nishi [1987: 156]</ref>.
== Legends and Natural Features == The shrine is famous for the ''Tsugizakura'' (Grafted Sakura), believed to have grown from the graft of a cypress and a cherry tree. A legend connects the tree to {{ill|Fujiwara no Hidehira|ja|藤原秀衡}}, a lord of the Northern Fujiwara clan, who is said to have left his newborn son near the shrine during his pilgrimage to Kumano, praying that if the child survived, the tree would flourish.
Another notable feature is the ''Nonaka Ippo Sugi'' (One-Sided Cedar of Nonaka), a grove of ancient cedar trees that grow with their branches leaning in the same direction. These trees, some over 800 years old, were preserved through the efforts of the naturalist {{ill|Minakata Kumagusu|ja|南方熊楠}}, who opposed the government’s shrine consolidation policies during the Meiji period.
== Nonaka Spring (Selected 100 Exquisite Waters of Japan) == Beneath the shrine lies the ''Nonaka Spring'', known for its clear waters that have never dried up. It served as a rest stop for pilgrims and remains a local water source. The spring is designated as a natural monument of Tanabe City.

revision.text:
'''Tsugizakura Ōji''' is one of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|fr|Kujūkuōji|ja|九十九王子|lt=99 ōji Shrines}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. <!--subst:PAGENAME magic word should be substituted in the future when this is moved to its final pagename. This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines--> ==Overview== {{Infobox Shinto shrine | name = Tsugizakura Ōji | image = [[File:Tsugizakura-oji and Ippo Sugi.JPG|250px]] | caption = Torii gate of Tsugizakura Ōji and the "Ippo Sugi" cedar | location = 591 Nonaka, Nakahechi-chō, Tanabe City, Wakayama Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{coord|33|49|42.7|N|135|38|03.0|E|region:JP}} | deity = Unknown | established = Unknown | other_names = Next Sakura Ōji, Continued Sakura Ōji | festivals = }}
'''Tsugizakura Ōji''' (継桜王子), also known as '''Next Sakura Ōji''' (次桜王子) or '''Continued Sakura Ōji''' (続桜王子), is a Shinto shrine located in {{ill|Nakahechi, Tanabe|ja|田辺市中辺路町}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|ja|和歌山県}}, Japan. It is one of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}} shrines along the {{ill|Kumano Kodo|ja|熊野古道}} pilgrimage route. The site is part of the UNESCO World Heritage-listed "Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range" and is designated as a National Historic Site of Japan (2000) and part of the Scenic Beauty Site "Southern Mandala Landscape" (2015)<ref name="Tanabe">{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html|title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments|publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education|accessdate=2016-05-21}}</ref>.
== History == [[File:Monument TSUGIZAKURA-oji remains.JPG|thumb|right|150px|Tsugizakura Ōji monument]] Tsugizakura Ōji is mentioned as early as 1109 in the ''{{ill|Chūyūki|ja|中右記}}'' and later in Fujiwara no Teika's ''Kumano Dō no Maguki'' (part of the ''Meigetsuki'') in 1201. The shrine is thought to have originally been located east of its current site and was relocated during the early modern period. During the Edo period, it was known as ''Wakaichi Ōji Gongen'' and served as the local guardian shrine. In 1909, it was merged with Chikano Shrine but later restored to its original status after World War II<ref name="Nishi">Nishi [1987: 156]</ref>.
== Legends and Natural Features == The shrine is famous for the ''Tsugizakura'' (Grafted Sakura), believed to have grown from the graft of a cypress and a cherry tree. A legend connects the tree to {{ill|Fujiwara no Hidehira|ja|藤原秀衡}}, a lord of the Northern Fujiwara clan, who is said to have left his newborn son near the shrine during his pilgrimage to Kumano, praying that if the child survived, the tree would flourish.
Another notable feature is the ''Nonaka Ippo Sugi'' (One-Sided Cedar of Nonaka), a grove of ancient cedar trees that grow with their branches leaning in the same direction. These trees, some over 800 years old, were preserved through the efforts of the naturalist {{ill|Minakata Kumagusu|ja|南方熊楠}}, who opposed the government’s shrine consolidation policies during the Meiji period.
== Nonaka Spring (Selected 100 Exquisite Waters of Japan) == Beneath the shrine lies the ''Nonaka Spring'', known for its clear waters that have never dried up. It served as a rest stop for pilgrims and remains a local water source. The spring is designated as a natural monument of Tanabe City.
== Cultural Properties == * **National Designations:** * Part of the "Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range" (Historic Site, 2000) * Part of the "Southern Mandala Landscape" (Place of Scenic Beauty, 2015)
* **Wakayama Prefecture Designations:** * Nonaka Ippo Sugi - Prefectural Natural Monument (1958) * Nonaka Lion Dance - Prefectural Folk Cultural Property (1971)
== Access == * **Address:** 591 Nonaka, Nakahechi-chō, Tanabe City, Wakayama Prefecture, Japan * **Transport:** From {{ill|Kii-Tanabe Station|ja|紀伊田辺駅}}, take a bus to the "Nonaka Ippo Sugi" stop, then walk about 10 minutes.
== References == * {{Cite book|ja|author=Ue Toshikatsu|year=2004|title=World Heritage Kumano Kodo|publisher=Shinjuku Shobō|isbn=4880083216}} * {{Cite book|ja|editor=Kadokawa Japanese Place Name Dictionary Editorial Committee|year=1985|title=Wakayama Prefecture|publisher=Kadokawa Shoten|isbn=404001300X}} * {{Cite book|ja|author=Kumanonji Editorial Committee|year=1973|title=Ancient Roads and Ōji Shrines - Kumano Nakahechi|publisher=Kumano Nakahechi Publishing Association}}
== External Links == * [http://www.nakahechi.jp/saijiki.html Nakahechi Seasonal Events] - Official site of the Nakahechi Tourism Association * [http://www.pref.wakayama.lg.jp/prefg/000200/photomuseum/087.html Tsugizakura Ōji] - Wakayama Prefecture Photo Museum

revision.text:
'''Tsugizakura Ōji''' is one of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|fr|Kujūkuōji|ja|九十九王子|lt=99 ōji Shrines}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. <!--subst:PAGENAME magic word should be substituted in the future when this is moved to its final pagename. This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines--> ==Overview== {{Infobox Shinto shrine | name = Tsugizakura Ōji | image = [[File:Tsugizakura-oji and Ippo Sugi.JPG|250px]] | caption = Torii gate of Tsugizakura Ōji and the "Ippo Sugi" cedar | location = 591 Nonaka, Nakahechi-chō, Tanabe City, Wakayama Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{coord|33|49|42.7|N|135|38|03.0|E|region:JP}} | deity = Unknown | established = Unknown | other_names = Next Sakura Ōji, Continued Sakura Ōji | festivals = }}
'''Tsugizakura Ōji''' (継桜王子), also known as '''Next Sakura Ōji''' (次桜王子) or '''Continued Sakura Ōji''' (続桜王子), is a Shinto shrine located in {{ill|Nakahechi, Tanabe|ja|田辺市中辺路町}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|ja|和歌山県}}, Japan. It is one of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}} shrines along the {{ill|Kumano Kodo|ja|熊野古道}} pilgrimage route. The site is part of the UNESCO World Heritage-listed "Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range" and is designated as a National Historic Site of Japan (2000) and part of the Scenic Beauty Site "Southern Mandala Landscape" (2015)<ref name="Tanabe">{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html|title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments|publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education|accessdate=2016-05-21}}</ref>.
== History == [[File:Monument TSUGIZAKURA-oji remains.JPG|thumb|right|150px|Tsugizakura Ōji monument]] Tsugizakura Ōji is mentioned as early as 1109 in the ''{{ill|Chūyūki|ja|中右記}}'' and later in Fujiwara no Teika's ''Kumano Dō no Maguki'' (part of the ''Meigetsuki'') in 1201. The shrine is thought to have originally been located east of its current site and was relocated during the early modern period. During the Edo period, it was known as ''Wakaichi Ōji Gongen'' and served as the local guardian shrine. In 1909, it was merged with Chikano Shrine but later restored to its original status after World War II<ref name="Nishi">Nishi [1987: 156]</ref>.
== Legends and Natural Features == The shrine is famous for the ''Tsugizakura'' (Grafted Sakura), believed to have grown from the graft of a cypress and a cherry tree. A legend connects the tree to {{ill|Fujiwara no Hidehira|ja|藤原秀衡}}, a lord of the Northern Fujiwara clan, who is said to have left his newborn son near the shrine during his pilgrimage to Kumano, praying that if the child survived, the tree would flourish.
Another notable feature is the ''Nonaka Ippo Sugi'' (One-Sided Cedar of Nonaka), a grove of ancient cedar trees that grow with their branches leaning in the same direction. These trees, some over 800 years old, were preserved through the efforts of the naturalist {{ill|Minakata Kumagusu|ja|南方熊楠}}, who opposed the government’s shrine consolidation policies during the Meiji period.
== Nonaka Spring (Selected 100 Exquisite Waters of Japan) == Beneath the shrine lies the ''Nonaka Spring'', known for its clear waters that have never dried up. It served as a rest stop for pilgrims and remains a local water source. The spring is designated as a natural monument of Tanabe City.
== Cultural Properties == * **National Designations:** * Part of the "Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range" (Historic Site, 2000) * Part of the "Southern Mandala Landscape" (Place of Scenic Beauty, 2015)
* **Wakayama Prefecture Designations:** * Nonaka Ippo Sugi - Prefectural Natural Monument (1958) * Nonaka Lion Dance - Prefectural Folk Cultural Property (1971)
== Access == * **Address:** 591 Nonaka, Nakahechi-chō, Tanabe City, Wakayama Prefecture, Japan * **Transport:** From {{ill|Kii-Tanabe Station|ja|紀伊田辺駅}}, take a bus to the "Nonaka Ippo Sugi" stop, then walk about 10 minutes.
== References == * {{Cite book|ja|author=Ue Toshikatsu|year=2004|title=World Heritage Kumano Kodo|publisher=Shinjuku Shobō|isbn=4880083216}} * {{Cite book|ja|editor=Kadokawa Japanese Place Name Dictionary Editorial Committee|year=1985|title=Wakayama Prefecture|publisher=Kadokawa Shoten|isbn=404001300X}} * {{Cite book|ja|author=Kumanonji Editorial Committee|year=1973|title=Ancient Roads and Ōji Shrines - Kumano Nakahechi|publisher=Kumano Nakahechi Publishing Association}}
== External Links == * [http://www.nakahechi.jp/saijiki.html Nakahechi Seasonal Events] - Official site of the Nakahechi Tourism Association * [http://www.pref.wakayama.lg.jp/prefg/000200/photomuseum/087.html Tsugizakura Ōji] - Wakayama Prefecture Photo Museum

'''Tsugizakura Ōji''' is one of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|fr|Kujūkuōji|ja|九十九王子|lt=99 ōji Shrines}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. <!--subst:PAGENAME magic word should be substituted in the future when this is moved to its final pagename. This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines--> ==Overview== {{Infobox Shinto shrine | name = Tsugizakura Ōji | image = [[File:Tsugizakura-oji and Ippo Sugi.JPG|250px]] | caption = Torii gate of Tsugizakura Ōji and the "Ippo Sugi" cedar | location = 591 Nonaka, Nakahechi-chō, Tanabe City, Wakayama Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{coord|33|49|42.7|N|135|38|03.0|E|region:JP}} | deity = Unknown | established = Unknown | other_names = Next Sakura Ōji, Continued Sakura Ōji | festivals = }}
'''Tsugizakura Ōji''' (継桜王子), also known as '''Next Sakura Ōji''' (次桜王子) or '''Continued Sakura Ōji''' (続桜王子), is a Shinto shrine located in {{ill|Nakahechi, Tanabe|ja|田辺市中辺路町}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|ja|和歌山県}}, Japan. It is one of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}} shrines along the {{ill|Kumano Kodo|ja|熊野古道}} pilgrimage route. The site is part of the UNESCO World Heritage-listed "Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range" and is designated as a National Historic Site of Japan (2000) and part of the Scenic Beauty Site "Southern Mandala Landscape" (2015)<ref name="Tanabe">{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html|title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments|publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education|accessdate=2016-05-21}}</ref>.
== History == [[File:Monument TSUGIZAKURA-oji remains.JPG|thumb|right|150px|Tsugizakura Ōji monument]] Tsugizakura Ōji is mentioned as early as 1109 in the ''{{ill|Chūyūki|ja|中右記}}'' and later in Fujiwara no Teika's ''Kumano Dō no Maguki'' (part of the ''Meigetsuki'') in 1201. The shrine is thought to have originally been located east of its current site and was relocated during the early modern period. During the Edo period, it was known as ''Wakaichi Ōji Gongen'' and served as the local guardian shrine. In 1909, it was merged with Chikano Shrine but later restored to its original status after World War II<ref name="Nishi">Nishi [1987: 156]</ref>.
== Legends and Natural Features == The shrine is famous for the ''Tsugizakura'' (Grafted Sakura), believed to have grown from the graft of a cypress and a cherry tree. A legend connects the tree to {{ill|Fujiwara no Hidehira|ja|藤原秀衡}}, a lord of the Northern Fujiwara clan, who is said to have left his newborn son near the shrine during his pilgrimage to Kumano, praying that if the child survived, the tree would flourish.
Another notable feature is the ''Nonaka Ippo Sugi'' (One-Sided Cedar of Nonaka), a grove of ancient cedar trees that grow with their branches leaning in the same direction. These trees, some over 800 years old, were preserved through the efforts of the naturalist {{ill|Minakata Kumagusu|ja|南方熊楠}}, who opposed the government’s shrine consolidation policies during the Meiji period.
== Nonaka Spring (Selected 100 Exquisite Waters of Japan) == Beneath the shrine lies the ''Nonaka Spring'', known for its clear waters that have never dried up. It served as a rest stop for pilgrims and remains a local water source. The spring is designated as a natural monument of Tanabe City.
== Cultural Properties == * **National Designations:** * Part of the "Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range" (Historic Site, 2000) * Part of the "Southern Mandala Landscape" (Place of Scenic Beauty, 2015)
* **Wakayama Prefecture Designations:** * Nonaka Ippo Sugi - Prefectural Natural Monument (1958) * Nonaka Lion Dance - Prefectural Folk Cultural Property (1971)
== Access == * **Address:** 591 Nonaka, Nakahechi-chō, Tanabe City, Wakayama Prefecture, Japan * **Transport:** From {{ill|Kii-Tanabe Station|ja|紀伊田辺駅}}, take a bus to the "Nonaka Ippo Sugi" stop, then walk about 10 minutes.
== References == * {{Cite book|ja|author=Ue Toshikatsu|year=2004|title=World Heritage Kumano Kodo|publisher=Shinjuku Shobō|isbn=4880083216}} * {{Cite book|ja|editor=Kadokawa Japanese Place Name Dictionary Editorial Committee|year=1985|title=Wakayama Prefecture|publisher=Kadokawa Shoten|isbn=404001300X}} * {{Cite book|ja|author=Kumanonji Editorial Committee|year=1973|title=Ancient Roads and Ōji Shrines - Kumano Nakahechi|publisher=Kumano Nakahechi Publishing Association}}

'''Tsugizakura Ōji''' is one of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|fr|Kujūkuōji|ja|九十九王子|lt=99 ōji Shrines}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. <!--subst:PAGENAME magic word should be substituted in the future when this is moved to its final pagename. This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines--> ==Overview== {{Infobox Shinto shrine | name = Tsugizakura Ōji | image = [[File:Tsugizakura-oji and Ippo Sugi.JPG|250px]] | caption = Torii gate of Tsugizakura Ōji and the "Ippo Sugi" cedar | location = 591 Nonaka, Nakahechi-chō, Tanabe City, Wakayama Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{coord|33|49|42.7|N|135|38|03.0|E|region:JP}} | deity = Unknown | established = Unknown | other_names = Next Sakura Ōji, Continued Sakura Ōji | festivals = }}
'''Tsugizakura Ōji''' (継桜王子), also known as '''Next Sakura Ōji''' (次桜王子) or '''Continued Sakura Ōji''' (続桜王子), is a Shinto shrine located in {{ill|Nakahechi, Tanabe|ja|田辺市中辺路町}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|ja|和歌山県}}, Japan. It is one of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}} shrines along the {{ill|Kumano Kodo|ja|熊野古道}} pilgrimage route. The site is part of the UNESCO World Heritage-listed "Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range" and is designated as a National Historic Site of Japan (2000) and part of the Scenic Beauty Site "Southern Mandala Landscape" (2015)<ref name="Tanabe">{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html|title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments|publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education|accessdate=2016-05-21}}</ref>.
== History == [[File:Monument TSUGIZAKURA-oji remains.JPG|thumb|right|150px|Tsugizakura Ōji monument]] Tsugizakura Ōji is mentioned as early as 1109 in the ''{{ill|Chūyūki|ja|中右記}}'' and later in Fujiwara no Teika's ''Kumano Dō no Maguki'' (part of the ''Meigetsuki'') in 1201. The shrine is thought to have originally been located east of its current site and was relocated during the early modern period. During the Edo period, it was known as ''Wakaichi Ōji Gongen'' and served as the local guardian shrine. In 1909, it was merged with Chikano Shrine but later restored to its original status after World War II<ref name="Nishi">Nishi [1987: 156]</ref>.
== Legends and Natural Features == The shrine is famous for the ''Tsugizakura'' (Grafted Sakura), believed to have grown from the graft of a cypress and a cherry tree. A legend connects the tree to {{ill|Fujiwara no Hidehira|ja|藤原秀衡}}, a lord of the Northern Fujiwara clan, who is said to have left his newborn son near the shrine during his pilgrimage to Kumano, praying that if the child survived, the tree would flourish.
Another notable feature is the ''Nonaka Ippo Sugi'' (One-Sided Cedar of Nonaka), a grove of ancient cedar trees that grow with their branches leaning in the same direction. These trees, some over 800 years old, were preserved through the efforts of the naturalist {{ill|Minakata Kumagusu|ja|南方熊楠}}, who opposed the government’s shrine consolidation policies during the Meiji period.
== Nonaka Spring (Selected 100 Exquisite Waters of Japan) == Beneath the shrine lies the ''Nonaka Spring'', known for its clear waters that have never dried up. It served as a rest stop for pilgrims and remains a local water source. The spring is designated as a natural monument of Tanabe City.
== Cultural Properties == * **National Designations:** * Part of the "Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range" (Historic Site, 2000) * Part of the "Southern Mandala Landscape" (Place of Scenic Beauty, 2015)
* **Wakayama Prefecture Designations:** * Nonaka Ippo Sugi - Prefectural Natural Monument (1958) * Nonaka Lion Dance - Prefectural Folk Cultural Property (1971)
== Access == * **Address:** 591 Nonaka, Nakahechi-chō, Tanabe City, Wakayama Prefecture, Japan * **Transport:** From {{ill|Kii-Tanabe Station|ja|紀伊田辺駅}}, take a bus to the "Nonaka Ippo Sugi" stop, then walk about 10 minutes.

'''Tsugizakura Ōji''' is one of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|fr|Kujūkuōji|ja|九十九王子|lt=99 ōji Shrines}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. <!--subst:PAGENAME magic word should be substituted in the future when this is moved to its final pagename. This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines--> ==Overview== {{Infobox Shinto shrine | name = Tsugizakura Ōji | image = [[File:Tsugizakura-oji and Ippo Sugi.JPG|250px]] | caption = Torii gate of Tsugizakura Ōji and the "Ippo Sugi" cedar | location = 591 Nonaka, Nakahechi-chō, Tanabe City, Wakayama Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{coord|33|49|42.7|N|135|38|03.0|E|region:JP}} | deity = Unknown | established = Unknown | other_names = Next Sakura Ōji, Continued Sakura Ōji | festivals = }}
'''Tsugizakura Ōji''' (継桜王子), also known as '''Next Sakura Ōji''' (次桜王子) or '''Continued Sakura Ōji''' (続桜王子), is a Shinto shrine located in {{ill|Nakahechi, Tanabe|ja|田辺市中辺路町}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|ja|和歌山県}}, Japan. It is one of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}} shrines along the {{ill|Kumano Kodo|ja|熊野古道}} pilgrimage route. The site is part of the UNESCO World Heritage-listed "Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range" and is designated as a National Historic Site of Japan (2000) and part of the Scenic Beauty Site "Southern Mandala Landscape" (2015)<ref name="Tanabe">{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html|title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments|publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education|accessdate=2016-05-21}}</ref>.
== History == [[File:Monument TSUGIZAKURA-oji remains.JPG|thumb|right|150px|Tsugizakura Ōji monument]] Tsugizakura Ōji is mentioned as early as 1109 in the ''{{ill|Chūyūki|ja|中右記}}'' and later in Fujiwara no Teika's ''Kumano Dō no Maguki'' (part of the ''Meigetsuki'') in 1201. The shrine is thought to have originally been located east of its current site and was relocated during the early modern period. During the Edo period, it was known as ''Wakaichi Ōji Gongen'' and served as the local guardian shrine. In 1909, it was merged with Chikano Shrine but later restored to its original status after World War II<ref name="Nishi">Nishi [1987: 156]</ref>.
== Legends and Natural Features == The shrine is famous for the ''Tsugizakura'' (Grafted Sakura), believed to have grown from the graft of a cypress and a cherry tree. A legend connects the tree to {{ill|Fujiwara no Hidehira|ja|藤原秀衡}}, a lord of the Northern Fujiwara clan, who is said to have left his newborn son near the shrine during his pilgrimage to Kumano, praying that if the child survived, the tree would flourish.
Another notable feature is the ''Nonaka Ippo Sugi'' (One-Sided Cedar of Nonaka), a grove of ancient cedar trees that grow with their branches leaning in the same direction. These trees, some over 800 years old, were preserved through the efforts of the naturalist {{ill|Minakata Kumagusu|ja|南方熊楠}}, who opposed the government’s shrine consolidation policies during the Meiji period.
== Nonaka Spring (Selected 100 Exquisite Waters of Japan) == Beneath the shrine lies the ''Nonaka Spring'', known for its clear waters that have never dried up. It served as a rest stop for pilgrims and remains a local water source. The spring is designated as a natural monument of Tanabe City.
== Cultural Properties == * **National Designations:** * Part of the "Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range" (Historic Site, 2000) * Part of the "Southern Mandala Landscape" (Place of Scenic Beauty, 2015)
* **Wakayama Prefecture Designations:** * Nonaka Ippo Sugi - Prefectural Natural Monument (1958) * Nonaka Lion Dance - Prefectural Folk Cultural Property (1971)
== Access == * **Address:** 591 Nonaka, Nakahechi-chō, Tanabe City, Wakayama Prefecture, Japan * **Transport:** From {{ill|Kii-Tanabe Station|ja|紀伊田辺駅}}, take a bus to the "Nonaka Ippo Sugi" stop, then walk about 10 minutes.

'''Tsugizakura Ōji''' is one of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|fr|Kujūkuōji|ja|九十九王子|lt=99 ōji Shrines}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. <!--subst:PAGENAME magic word should be substituted in the future when this is moved to its final pagename. This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines--> ==Overview== {{Infobox Shinto shrine | name = Tsugizakura Ōji | image = [[File:Tsugizakura-oji and Ippo Sugi.JPG|250px]] | caption = Torii gate of Tsugizakura Ōji and the "Ippo Sugi" cedar | location = 591 Nonaka, Nakahechi-chō, Tanabe City, Wakayama Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{coord|33|49|42.7|N|135|38|03.0|E|region:JP}} | deity = Unknown | established = Unknown | other_names = Next Sakura Ōji, Continued Sakura Ōji | festivals = }}
'''Tsugizakura Ōji''' (継桜王子), also known as '''Next Sakura Ōji''' (次桜王子) or '''Continued Sakura Ōji''' (続桜王子), is a Shinto shrine located in {{ill|Nakahechi, Tanabe|ja|田辺市中辺路町}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|ja|和歌山県}}, Japan. It is one of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}} shrines along the {{ill|Kumano Kodo|ja|熊野古道}} pilgrimage route. The site is part of the UNESCO World Heritage-listed "Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range" and is designated as a National Historic Site of Japan (2000) and part of the Scenic Beauty Site "Southern Mandala Landscape" (2015)<ref name="Tanabe">{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html|title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments|publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education|accessdate=2016-05-21}}</ref>.
== History == [[File:Monument TSUGIZAKURA-oji remains.JPG|thumb|right|150px|Tsugizakura Ōji monument]] Tsugizakura Ōji is mentioned as early as 1109 in the ''{{ill|Chūyūki|ja|中右記}}'' and later in Fujiwara no Teika's ''Kumano Dō no Maguki'' (part of the ''Meigetsuki'') in 1201. The shrine is thought to have originally been located east of its current site and was relocated during the early modern period. During the Edo period, it was known as ''Wakaichi Ōji Gongen'' and served as the local guardian shrine. In 1909, it was merged with Chikano Shrine but later restored to its original status after World War II<ref name="Nishi">Nishi [1987: 156]</ref>.
== Legends and Natural Features == The shrine is famous for the ''Tsugizakura'' (Grafted Sakura), believed to have grown from the graft of a cypress and a cherry tree. A legend connects the tree to {{ill|Fujiwara no Hidehira|ja|藤原秀衡}}, a lord of the Northern Fujiwara clan, who is said to have left his newborn son near the shrine during his pilgrimage to Kumano, praying that if the child survived, the tree would flourish.
Another notable feature is the ''Nonaka Ippo Sugi'' (One-Sided Cedar of Nonaka), a grove of ancient cedar trees that grow with their branches leaning in the same direction. These trees, some over 800 years old, were preserved through the efforts of the naturalist {{ill|Minakata Kumagusu|ja|南方熊楠}}, who opposed the government’s shrine consolidation policies during the Meiji period.
== Nonaka Spring (Selected 100 Exquisite Waters of Japan) == Beneath the shrine lies the ''Nonaka Spring'', known for its clear waters that have never dried up. It served as a rest stop for pilgrims and remains a local water source. The spring is designated as a natural monument of Tanabe City.
== Cultural Properties == * **National Designations:** * Part of the "Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range" (Historic Site, 2000) * Part of the "Southern Mandala Landscape" (Place of Scenic Beauty, 2015)
* **Wakayama Prefecture Designations:** * Nonaka Ippo Sugi - Prefectural Natural Monument (1958) * Nonaka Lion Dance - Prefectural Folk Cultural Property (1971)
== Access == * **Address:** 591 Nonaka, Nakahechi-chō, Tanabe City, Wakayama Prefecture, Japan * **Transport:** From {{ill|Kii-Tanabe Station|ja|紀伊田辺駅}}, take a bus to the "Nonaka Ippo Sugi" stop, then walk about 10 minutes.

'''Tsugizakura Ōji''' is one of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|fr|Kujūkuōji|ja|九十九王子|lt=99 ōji Shrines}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. <!--subst:PAGENAME magic word should be substituted in the future when this is moved to its final pagename. This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines--> ==Overview== {{Infobox Shinto shrine | name = Tsugizakura Ōji | image = [[File:Tsugizakura-oji and Ippo Sugi.JPG|250px]] | caption = Torii gate of Tsugizakura Ōji and the "Ippo Sugi" cedar | location = 591 Nonaka, Nakahechi-chō, Tanabe City, Wakayama Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{coord|33|49|42.7|N|135|38|03.0|E|region:JP}} | deity = Unknown | established = Unknown | other_names = Next Sakura Ōji, Continued Sakura Ōji | festivals = }}
'''Tsugizakura Ōji''' (継桜王子), also known as '''Next Sakura Ōji''' (次桜王子) or '''Continued Sakura Ōji''' (続桜王子), is a Shinto shrine located in {{ill|Nakahechi, Tanabe|ja|田辺市中辺路町}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|ja|和歌山県}}, Japan. It is one of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}} shrines along the {{ill|Kumano Kodo|ja|熊野古道}} pilgrimage route. The site is part of the UNESCO World Heritage-listed "Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range" and is designated as a National Historic Site of Japan (2000) and part of the Scenic Beauty Site "Southern Mandala Landscape" (2015)<ref name="Tanabe">{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html|title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments|publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education|accessdate=2016-05-21}}</ref>.
== History == [[File:Monument TSUGIZAKURA-oji remains.JPG|thumb|right|150px|Tsugizakura Ōji monument]] Tsugizakura Ōji is mentioned as early as 1109 in the ''{{ill|Chūyūki|ja|中右記}}'' and later in Fujiwara no Teika's ''Kumano Dō no Maguki'' (part of the ''Meigetsuki'') in 1201. The shrine is thought to have originally been located east of its current site and was relocated during the early modern period. During the Edo period, it was known as ''Wakaichi Ōji Gongen'' and served as the local guardian shrine. In 1909, it was merged with Chikano Shrine but later restored to its original status after World War II<ref name="Nishi">Nishi [1987: 156]</ref>.
== Legends and Natural Features == The shrine is famous for the ''Tsugizakura'' (Grafted Sakura), believed to have grown from the graft of a cypress and a cherry tree. A legend connects the tree to {{ill|Fujiwara no Hidehira|ja|藤原秀衡}}, a lord of the Northern Fujiwara clan, who is said to have left his newborn son near the shrine during his pilgrimage to Kumano, praying that if the child survived, the tree would flourish.
Another notable feature is the ''Nonaka Ippo Sugi'' (One-Sided Cedar of Nonaka), a grove of ancient cedar trees that grow with their branches leaning in the same direction. These trees, some over 800 years old, were preserved through the efforts of the naturalist {{ill|Minakata Kumagusu|ja|南方熊楠}}, who opposed the government’s shrine consolidation policies during the Meiji period.
== Nonaka Spring (Selected 100 Exquisite Waters of Japan) == Beneath the shrine lies the ''Nonaka Spring'', known for its clear waters that have never dried up. It served as a rest stop for pilgrims and remains a local water source. The spring is designated as a natural monument of Tanabe City.
== Cultural Properties == * **National Designations:** * Part of the "Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range" (Historic Site, 2000) * Part of the "Southern Mandala Landscape" (Place of Scenic Beauty, 2015)
* **Wakayama Prefecture Designations:** * Nonaka Ippo Sugi - Prefectural Natural Monument (1958) * Nonaka Lion Dance - Prefectural Folk Cultural Property (1971)
== Access == * **Address:** 591 Nonaka, Nakahechi-chō, Tanabe City, Wakayama Prefecture, Japan * **Transport:** From {{ill|Kii-Tanabe Station|ja|紀伊田辺駅}}, take a bus to the "Nonaka Ippo Sugi" stop, then walk about 10 minutes.

'''Tsugizakura Ōji''' is one of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|fr|Kujūkuōji|ja|九十九王子|lt=99 ōji Shrines}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. <!--subst:PAGENAME magic word should be substituted in the future when this is moved to its final pagename. This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines--> ==Overview== {{Infobox Shinto shrine | name = Tsugizakura Ōji | image = [[File:Tsugizakura-oji and Ippo Sugi.JPG|250px]] | caption = Torii gate of Tsugizakura Ōji and the "Ippo Sugi" cedar | location = 591 Nonaka, Nakahechi-chō, Tanabe City, Wakayama Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{coord|33|49|42.7|N|135|38|03.0|E|region:JP}} | deity = Unknown | established = Unknown | other_names = Next Sakura Ōji, Continued Sakura Ōji | festivals = }}
'''Tsugizakura Ōji''' (継桜王子), also known as '''Next Sakura Ōji''' (次桜王子) or '''Continued Sakura Ōji''' (続桜王子), is a Shinto shrine located in {{ill|Nakahechi, Tanabe|ja|田辺市中辺路町}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|ja|和歌山県}}, Japan. It is one of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}} shrines along the {{ill|Kumano Kodo|ja|熊野古道}} pilgrimage route. The site is part of the UNESCO World Heritage-listed "Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range" and is designated as a National Historic Site of Japan (2000) and part of the Scenic Beauty Site "Southern Mandala Landscape" (2015)<ref name="Tanabe">{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html|title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments|publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education|accessdate=2016-05-21}}</ref>.
== History == [[File:Monument TSUGIZAKURA-oji remains.JPG|thumb|right|150px|Tsugizakura Ōji monument]] Tsugizakura Ōji is mentioned as early as 1109 in the ''{{ill|Chūyūki|ja|中右記}}'' and later in Fujiwara no Teika's ''Kumano Dō no Maguki'' (part of the ''Meigetsuki'') in 1201. The shrine is thought to have originally been located east of its current site and was relocated during the early modern period. During the Edo period, it was known as ''Wakaichi Ōji Gongen'' and served as the local guardian shrine. In 1909, it was merged with Chikano Shrine but later restored to its original status after World War II<ref name="Nishi">Nishi [1987: 156]</ref>.
== Legends and Natural Features == The shrine is famous for the ''Tsugizakura'' (Grafted Sakura), believed to have grown from the graft of a cypress and a cherry tree. A legend connects the tree to {{ill|Fujiwara no Hidehira|ja|藤原秀衡}}, a lord of the Northern Fujiwara clan, who is said to have left his newborn son near the shrine during his pilgrimage to Kumano, praying that if the child survived, the tree would flourish.
Another notable feature is the ''Nonaka Ippo Sugi'' (One-Sided Cedar of Nonaka), a grove of ancient cedar trees that grow with their branches leaning in the same direction. These trees, some over 800 years old, were preserved through the efforts of the naturalist {{ill|Minakata Kumagusu|ja|南方熊楠}}, who opposed the government’s shrine consolidation policies during the Meiji period.
== Nonaka Spring (Selected 100 Exquisite Waters of Japan) == Beneath the shrine lies the ''Nonaka Spring'', known for its clear waters that have never dried up. It served as a rest stop for pilgrims and remains a local water source. The spring is designated as a natural monument of Tanabe City.
== Cultural Properties == * **National Designations:** * Part of the "Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range" (Historic Site, 2000) * Part of the "Southern Mandala Landscape" (Place of Scenic Beauty, 2015)
* **Wakayama Prefecture Designations:** * Nonaka Ippo Sugi - Prefectural Natural Monument (1958) * Nonaka Lion Dance - Prefectural Folk Cultural Property (1971)
== Access == * **Address:** 591 Nonaka, Nakahechi-chō, Tanabe City, Wakayama Prefecture, Japan * **Transport:** From {{ill|Kii-Tanabe Station|ja|紀伊田辺駅}}, take a bus to the "Nonaka Ippo Sugi" stop, then walk about 10 minutes.

This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines--> ==Overview== {{Infobox Shinto shrine | name = Tsugizakura Ōji | image = [[File:Tsugizakura-oji and Ippo Sugi.JPG|250px]] | caption = Torii gate of Tsugizakura Ōji and the "Ippo Sugi" cedar | location = 591 Nonaka, Nakahechi-chō, Tanabe City, Wakayama Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{coord|33|49|42.7|N|135|38|03.0|E|region:JP}} | deity = Unknown | established = Unknown | other_names = Next Sakura Ōji, Continued Sakura Ōji | festivals = }}
'''Tsugizakura Ōji''' (継桜王子), also known as '''Next Sakura Ōji''' (次桜王子) or '''Continued Sakura Ōji''' (続桜王子), is a Shinto shrine located in {{ill|Nakahechi, Tanabe|ja|田辺市中辺路町}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|ja|和歌山県}}, Japan. It is one of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}} shrines along the {{ill|Kumano Kodo|ja|熊野古道}} pilgrimage route. The site is part of the UNESCO World Heritage-listed "Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range" and is designated as a National Historic Site of Japan (2000) and part of the Scenic Beauty Site "Southern Mandala Landscape" (2015)<ref name="Tanabe">{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html|title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments|publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education|accessdate=2016-05-21}}</ref>.
== History == [[File:Monument TSUGIZAKURA-oji remains.JPG|thumb|right|150px|Tsugizakura Ōji monument]] Tsugizakura Ōji is mentioned as early as 1109 in the ''{{ill|Chūyūki|ja|中右記}}'' and later in Fujiwara no Teika's ''Kumano Dō no Maguki'' (part of the ''Meigetsuki'') in 1201. The shrine is thought to have originally been located east of its current site and was relocated during the early modern period. During the Edo period, it was known as ''Wakaichi Ōji Gongen'' and served as the local guardian shrine. In 1909, it was merged with Chikano Shrine but later restored to its original status after World War II<ref name="Nishi">Nishi [1987: 156]</ref>.
== Legends and Natural Features == The shrine is famous for the ''Tsugizakura'' (Grafted Sakura), believed to have grown from the graft of a cypress and a cherry tree. A legend connects the tree to {{ill|Fujiwara no Hidehira|ja|藤原秀衡}}, a lord of the Northern Fujiwara clan, who is said to have left his newborn son near the shrine during his pilgrimage to Kumano, praying that if the child survived, the tree would flourish.
Another notable feature is the ''Nonaka Ippo Sugi'' (One-Sided Cedar of Nonaka), a grove of ancient cedar trees that grow with their branches leaning in the same direction. These trees, some over 800 years old, were preserved through the efforts of the naturalist {{ill|Minakata Kumagusu|ja|南方熊楠}}, who opposed the government’s shrine consolidation policies during the Meiji period.
== Nonaka Spring (Selected 100 Exquisite Waters of Japan) == Beneath the shrine lies the ''Nonaka Spring'', known for its clear waters that have never dried up. It served as a rest stop for pilgrims and remains a local water source. The spring is designated as a natural monument of Tanabe City.
== Cultural Properties == * **National Designations:** * Part of the "Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range" (Historic Site, 2000) * Part of the "Southern Mandala Landscape" (Place of Scenic Beauty, 2015)
* **Wakayama Prefecture Designations:** * Nonaka Ippo Sugi - Prefectural Natural Monument (1958) * Nonaka Lion Dance - Prefectural Folk Cultural Property (1971)
== Access == * **Address:** 591 Nonaka, Nakahechi-chō, Tanabe City, Wakayama Prefecture, Japan * **Transport:** From {{ill|Kii-Tanabe Station|ja|紀伊田辺駅}}, take a bus to the "Nonaka Ippo Sugi" stop, then walk about 10 minutes.

'''Tsugizakura Ōji''' is one of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|fr|Kujūkuōji|ja|九十九王子|lt=99 ōji Shrines}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. <!--subst:PAGENAME magic word should be substituted in the future when this is moved to its final pagename. This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines--> ==Overview== {{Infobox Shinto shrine | name = Tsugizakura Ōji | image = [[File:Tsugizakura-oji and Ippo Sugi.JPG|250px]] | caption = Torii gate of Tsugizakura Ōji and the "Ippo Sugi" cedar | location = 591 Nonaka, Nakahechi-chō, Tanabe City, Wakayama Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{coord|33|49|42.7|N|135|38|03.0|E|region:JP}} | deity = Unknown | established = Unknown | other_names = Next Sakura Ōji, Continued Sakura Ōji | festivals = }}
'''Tsugizakura Ōji''' (継桜王子), also known as '''Next Sakura Ōji''' (次桜王子) or '''Continued Sakura Ōji''' (続桜王子), is a Shinto shrine located in {{ill|Nakahechi, Tanabe|ja|田辺市中辺路町}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|ja|和歌山県}}, Japan. It is one of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}} shrines along the {{ill|Kumano Kodo|ja|熊野古道}} pilgrimage route. The site is part of the UNESCO World Heritage-listed "Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range" and is designated as a National Historic Site of Japan (2000) and part of the Scenic Beauty Site "Southern Mandala Landscape" (2015)<ref name="Tanabe">{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html|title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments|publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education|accessdate=2016-05-21}}</ref>.
== History == [[File:Monument TSUGIZAKURA-oji remains.JPG|thumb|right|150px|Tsugizakura Ōji monument]] Tsugizakura Ōji is mentioned as early as 1109 in the ''{{ill|Chūyūki|ja|中右記}}'' and later in Fujiwara no Teika's ''Kumano Dō no Maguki'' (part of the ''Meigetsuki'') in 1201. The shrine is thought to have originally been located east of its current site and was relocated during the early modern period. During the Edo period, it was known as ''Wakaichi Ōji Gongen'' and served as the local guardian shrine. In 1909, it was merged with Chikano Shrine but later restored to its original status after World War II<ref name="Nishi">Nishi [1987: 156]</ref>.
== Legends and Natural Features == The shrine is famous for the ''Tsugizakura'' (Grafted Sakura), believed to have grown from the graft of a cypress and a cherry tree. A legend connects the tree to {{ill|Fujiwara no Hidehira|ja|藤原秀衡}}, a lord of the Northern Fujiwara clan, who is said to have left his newborn son near the shrine during his pilgrimage to Kumano, praying that if the child survived, the tree would flourish.
Another notable feature is the ''Nonaka Ippo Sugi'' (One-Sided Cedar of Nonaka), a grove of ancient cedar trees that grow with their branches leaning in the same direction. These trees, some over 800 years old, were preserved through the efforts of the naturalist {{ill|Minakata Kumagusu|ja|南方熊楠}}, who opposed the government’s shrine consolidation policies during the Meiji period.
== Nonaka Spring (Selected 100 Exquisite Waters of Japan) == Beneath the shrine lies the ''Nonaka Spring'', known for its clear waters that have never dried up. It served as a rest stop for pilgrims and remains a local water source. The spring is designated as a natural monument of Tanabe City.
== Cultural Properties == * **National Designations:** * Part of the "Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range" (Historic Site, 2000) * Part of the "Southern Mandala Landscape" (Place of Scenic Beauty, 2015)
* **Wakayama Prefecture Designations:** * Nonaka Ippo Sugi - Prefectural Natural Monument (1958) * Nonaka Lion Dance - Prefectural Folk Cultural Property (1971)
== Access == * **Address:** 591 Nonaka, Nakahechi-chō, Tanabe City, Wakayama Prefecture, Japan * **Transport:** From {{ill|Kii-Tanabe Station|ja|紀伊田辺駅}}, take a bus to the "Nonaka Ippo Sugi" stop, then walk about 10 minutes.

'''Tsugizakura Ōji''' is one of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|fr|Kujūkuōji|ja|九十九王子|lt=99 ōji Shrines}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. <!--subst:PAGENAME magic word should be substituted in the future when this is moved to its final pagename. This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines--> ==Overview== {{Infobox Shinto shrine | name = Tsugizakura Ōji | image = [[File:Tsugizakura-oji and Ippo Sugi.JPG|250px]] | caption = Torii gate of Tsugizakura Ōji and the "Ippo Sugi" cedar | location = 591 Nonaka, Nakahechi-chō, Tanabe City, Wakayama Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{coord|33|49|42.7|N|135|38|03.0|E|region:JP}} | deity = Unknown | established = Unknown | other_names = Next Sakura Ōji, Continued Sakura Ōji | festivals = }}
'''Tsugizakura Ōji''' (継桜王子), also known as '''Next Sakura Ōji''' (次桜王子) or '''Continued Sakura Ōji''' (続桜王子), is a Shinto shrine located in {{ill|Nakahechi, Tanabe|ja|田辺市中辺路町}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|ja|和歌山県}}, Japan. It is one of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}} shrines along the {{ill|Kumano Kodo|ja|熊野古道}} pilgrimage route. The site is part of the UNESCO World Heritage-listed "Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range" and is designated as a National Historic Site of Japan (2000) and part of the Scenic Beauty Site "Southern Mandala Landscape" (2015)<ref name="Tanabe">{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html|title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments|publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education|accessdate=2016-05-21}}</ref>.
== History == [[File:Monument TSUGIZAKURA-oji remains.JPG|thumb|right|150px|Tsugizakura Ōji monument]] Tsugizakura Ōji is mentioned as early as 1109 in the ''{{ill|Chūyūki|ja|中右記}}'' and later in Fujiwara no Teika's ''Kumano Dō no Maguki'' (part of the ''Meigetsuki'') in 1201. The shrine is thought to have originally been located east of its current site and was relocated during the early modern period. During the Edo period, it was known as ''Wakaichi Ōji Gongen'' and served as the local guardian shrine. In 1909, it was merged with Chikano Shrine but later restored to its original status after World War II<ref name="Nishi">Nishi [1987: 156]</ref>.
== Legends and Natural Features == The shrine is famous for the ''Tsugizakura'' (Grafted Sakura), believed to have grown from the graft of a cypress and a cherry tree. A legend connects the tree to {{ill|Fujiwara no Hidehira|ja|藤原秀衡}}, a lord of the Northern Fujiwara clan, who is said to have left his newborn son near the shrine during his pilgrimage to Kumano, praying that if the child survived, the tree would flourish.
Another notable feature is the ''Nonaka Ippo Sugi'' (One-Sided Cedar of Nonaka), a grove of ancient cedar trees that grow with their branches leaning in the same direction. These trees, some over 800 years old, were preserved through the efforts of the naturalist {{ill|Minakata Kumagusu|ja|南方熊楠}}, who opposed the government’s shrine consolidation policies during the Meiji period.
== Nonaka Spring (Selected 100 Exquisite Waters of Japan) == Beneath the shrine lies the ''Nonaka Spring'', known for its clear waters that have never dried up. It served as a rest stop for pilgrims and remains a local water source. The spring is designated as a natural monument of Tanabe City.
== Cultural Properties == * **National Designations:** * Part of the "Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range" (Historic Site, 2000) * Part of the "Southern Mandala Landscape" (Place of Scenic Beauty, 2015)
* **Wakayama Prefecture Designations:** * Nonaka Ippo Sugi - Prefectural Natural Monument (1958) * Nonaka Lion Dance - Prefectural Folk Cultural Property (1971)
== Access == * **Address:** 591 Nonaka, Nakahechi-chō, Tanabe City, Wakayama Prefecture, Japan * **Transport:** From {{ill|Kii-Tanabe Station|ja|紀伊田辺駅}}, take a bus to the "Nonaka Ippo Sugi" stop, then walk about 10 minutes.

'''Tsugizakura Ōji''' is one of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|fr|Kujūkuōji|ja|九十九王子|lt=99 ōji Shrines}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. <!--subst:PAGENAME magic word should be substituted in the future when this is moved to its final pagename. This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines--> ==Overview== {{Infobox Shinto shrine | name = Tsugizakura Ōji | image = [[File:Tsugizakura-oji and Ippo Sugi.JPG|250px]] | caption = Torii gate of Tsugizakura Ōji and the "Ippo Sugi" cedar | location = 591 Nonaka, Nakahechi-chō, Tanabe City, Wakayama Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{coord|33|49|42.7|N|135|38|03.0|E|region:JP}} | deity = Unknown | established = Unknown | other_names = Next Sakura Ōji, Continued Sakura Ōji | festivals = }}
'''Tsugizakura Ōji''' (継桜王子), also known as '''Next Sakura Ōji''' (次桜王子) or '''Continued Sakura Ōji''' (続桜王子), is a Shinto shrine located in {{ill|Nakahechi, Tanabe|ja|田辺市中辺路町}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|ja|和歌山県}}, Japan. It is one of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}} shrines along the {{ill|Kumano Kodo|ja|熊野古道}} pilgrimage route. The site is part of the UNESCO World Heritage-listed "Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range" and is designated as a National Historic Site of Japan (2000) and part of the Scenic Beauty Site "Southern Mandala Landscape" (2015)<ref name="Tanabe">{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html|title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments|publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education|accessdate=2016-05-21}}</ref>.
== History == [[File:Monument TSUGIZAKURA-oji remains.JPG|thumb|right|150px|Tsugizakura Ōji monument]] Tsugizakura Ōji is mentioned as early as 1109 in the ''{{ill|Chūyūki|ja|中右記}}'' and later in Fujiwara no Teika's ''Kumano Dō no Maguki'' (part of the ''Meigetsuki'') in 1201. The shrine is thought to have originally been located east of its current site and was relocated during the early modern period. During the Edo period, it was known as ''Wakaichi Ōji Gongen'' and served as the local guardian shrine. In 1909, it was merged with Chikano Shrine but later restored to its original status after World War II<ref name="Nishi">Nishi [1987: 156]</ref>.
== Legends and Natural Features == The shrine is famous for the ''Tsugizakura'' (Grafted Sakura), believed to have grown from the graft of a cypress and a cherry tree. A legend connects the tree to {{ill|Fujiwara no Hidehira|ja|藤原秀衡}}, a lord of the Northern Fujiwara clan, who is said to have left his newborn son near the shrine during his pilgrimage to Kumano, praying that if the child survived, the tree would flourish.
Another notable feature is the ''Nonaka Ippo Sugi'' (One-Sided Cedar of Nonaka), a grove of ancient cedar trees that grow with their branches leaning in the same direction. These trees, some over 800 years old, were preserved through the efforts of the naturalist {{ill|Minakata Kumagusu|ja|南方熊楠}}, who opposed the government’s shrine consolidation policies during the Meiji period.
== Nonaka Spring (Selected 100 Exquisite Waters of Japan) == Beneath the shrine lies the ''Nonaka Spring'', known for its clear waters that have never dried up. It served as a rest stop for pilgrims and remains a local water source. The spring is designated as a natural monument of Tanabe City.
== Cultural Properties == * **National Designations:** * Part of the "Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range" (Historic Site, 2000) * Part of the "Southern Mandala Landscape" (Place of Scenic Beauty, 2015)
* **Wakayama Prefecture Designations:** * Nonaka Ippo Sugi - Prefectural Natural Monument (1958) * Nonaka Lion Dance - Prefectural Folk Cultural Property (1971)
== Access == * **Address:** 591 Nonaka, Nakahechi-chō, Tanabe City, Wakayama Prefecture, Japan * **Transport:** From {{ill|Kii-Tanabe Station|ja|紀伊田辺駅}}, take a bus to the "Nonaka Ippo Sugi" stop, then walk about 10 minutes.

'''Tsugizakura Ōji''' is one of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|fr|Kujūkuōji|ja|九十九王子|lt=99 ōji Shrines}} on the [[Kumano Kodō]]. <!--subst:PAGENAME magic word should be substituted in the future when this is moved to its final pagename. This was added to a few pages not created on Feb 8 because they were very barren and this gives context to the fact that they are in a large group of pages all to be translated more or less as a group similar to the Ise Shrines--> ==Overview== {{Infobox Shinto shrine | name = Tsugizakura Ōji | image = [[File:Tsugizakura-oji and Ippo Sugi.JPG|250px]] | caption = Torii gate of Tsugizakura Ōji and the "Ippo Sugi" cedar | location = 591 Nonaka, Nakahechi-chō, Tanabe City, Wakayama Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{coord|33|49|42.7|N|135|38|03.0|E|region:JP}} | deity = Unknown | established = Unknown | other_names = Next Sakura Ōji, Continued Sakura Ōji | festivals = }}
'''Tsugizakura Ōji''' (継桜王子), also known as '''Next Sakura Ōji''' (次桜王子) or '''Continued Sakura Ōji''' (続桜王子), is a Shinto shrine located in {{ill|Nakahechi, Tanabe|ja|田辺市中辺路町}}, {{ill|Wakayama Prefecture|ja|和歌山県}}, Japan. It is one of the {{ill|Kujūku Ōji|ja|九十九王子}} shrines along the {{ill|Kumano Kodo|ja|熊野古道}} pilgrimage route. The site is part of the UNESCO World Heritage-listed "Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range" and is designated as a National Historic Site of Japan (2000) and part of the Scenic Beauty Site "Southern Mandala Landscape" (2015)<ref name="Tanabe">{{Cite web|ja|url=https://www.city.tanabe.lg.jp/bunshin/bunkazai/shiteibunkazai_kinenbutsu.html|title=Designated Cultural Properties of Tanabe City - Monuments|publisher=Tanabe City Board of Education|accessdate=2016-05-21}}</ref>.
== History == [[File:Monument TSUGIZAKURA-oji remains.JPG|thumb|right|150px|Tsugizakura Ōji monument]] Tsugizakura Ōji is mentioned as early as 1109 in the ''{{ill|Chūyūki|ja|中右記}}'' and later in Fujiwara no Teika's ''Kumano Dō no Maguki'' (part of the ''Meigetsuki'') in 1201. The shrine is thought to have originally been located east of its current site and was relocated during the early modern period. During the Edo period, it was known as ''Wakaichi Ōji Gongen'' and served as the local guardian shrine. In 1909, it was merged with Chikano Shrine but later restored to its original status after World War II<ref name="Nishi">Nishi [1987: 156]</ref>.
== Legends and Natural Features == The shrine is famous for the ''Tsugizakura'' (Grafted Sakura), believed to have grown from the graft of a cypress and a cherry tree. A legend connects the tree to {{ill|Fujiwara no Hidehira|ja|藤原秀衡}}, a lord of the Northern Fujiwara clan, who is said to have left his newborn son near the shrine during his pilgrimage to Kumano, praying that if the child survived, the tree would flourish.
Another notable feature is the ''Nonaka Ippo Sugi'' (One-Sided Cedar of Nonaka), a grove of ancient cedar trees that grow with their branches leaning in the same direction. These trees, some over 800 years old, were preserved through the efforts of the naturalist {{ill|Minakata Kumagusu|ja|南方熊楠}}, who opposed the government’s shrine consolidation policies during the Meiji period.
== Nonaka Spring (Selected 100 Exquisite Waters of Japan) == Beneath the shrine lies the ''Nonaka Spring'', known for its clear waters that have never dried up. It served as a rest stop for pilgrims and remains a local water source. The spring is designated as a natural monument of Tanabe City.
== Cultural Properties == * **National Designations:** * Part of the "Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range" (Historic Site, 2000) * Part of the "Southern Mandala Landscape" (Place of Scenic Beauty, 2015)
* **Wakayama Prefecture Designations:** * Nonaka Ippo Sugi - Prefectural Natural Monument (1958) * Nonaka Lion Dance - Prefectural Folk Cultural Property (1971)
== Access == * **Address:** 591 Nonaka, Nakahechi-chō, Tanabe City, Wakayama Prefecture, Japan * **Transport:** From {{ill|Kii-Tanabe Station|ja|紀伊田辺駅}}, take a bus to the "Nonaka Ippo Sugi" stop, then walk about 10 minutes.
== References == * {{Cite book|ja|author=Ue Toshikatsu|year=2004|title=World Heritage Kumano Kodo|publisher=Shinjuku Shobō|isbn=4880083216}} * {{Cite book|ja|editor=Kadokawa Japanese Place Name Dictionary Editorial Committee|year=1985|title=Wakayama Prefecture|publisher=Kadokawa Shoten|isbn=404001300X}} * {{Cite book|ja|author=Kumanonji Editorial Committee|year=1973|title=Ancient Roads and Ōji Shrines - Kumano Nakahechi|publisher=Kumano Nakahechi Publishing Association}}
== External Links == * [http://www.nakahechi.jp/saijiki.html Nakahechi Seasonal Events] - Official site of the Nakahechi Tourism Association * [http://www.pref.wakayama.lg.jp/prefg/000200/photomuseum/087.html Tsugizakura Ōji] - Wakayama Prefecture Photo Museum
